Q125566596.summary: Beneath an openwork canopy carried on spirally fluted columns, Christ stands upright on the cross, his feet resting on a footrest and his arms stretched wide. The Virgin reaches out both hands toward her Son, while Saint John, holding a book, raises his right hand; beneath the cross a shell-like form suggests the hill of Golgotha. Carved in Constantinople, this small, worn relief was once the centre of a portable triptych for private prayer.
facts: The museum records drill holes in the upper and lower frame that once secured mounts for the now-lost wings, confirming that the plaque was the centre of a triptych.
The upper arm of the cross was left blank for an inscription, as noted in the museum's description.
The museum dates the ivory to the second half of the 10th century and attributes it to Constantinople.
Q125566596.notes: Inv. Pl.O.475; H. 12.9 cm, W. 11.2 cm. Worklist object type 'triptych' changed to 'ivory' because only the central panel survives.

commons:90992106.summary: Within a shallow arched niche, lit against the rough tufa of the rock-cut church, the Virgin in a dark maphorion bends her head towards the Christ Child, who sits on her arm in an ochre garment and presses his face close to hers; both wear golden haloes, and the dark blue ground is scattered with small white stars. Above and around the niche the deep blue paintings of the New Church can be glimpsed. The tender, cheek-to-cheek embrace belongs to the Byzantine type of the Virgin of tenderness (Eleousa).
facts: Tokalı Kilise, the largest church at Göreme, consists of an Old Church of the early 10th century and a larger New Church added later in the century, whose paintings use costly lapis-lazuli blue.
An inscription names the painter of the New Church as Nikephoros and its patrons as Constantine and his son Leon.

links.label: Wikimedia Commons: Frescos in the Tokalı Kilise

commons:90992106.notes: Commons descriptions (two independent photographers) date this niche painting to the 10th century; the Princeton Index of Medieval Art records an Eleousa Virgin and Child on the sanctuary east wall. Its exact phase (New Church c. 950–970, or later) is not confirmed; the New Church itself is dated variously from c. 960 to the end of the 10th or early 11th century.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-27-christ.summary: The psalmist, as a king, raises his hands toward a tabernacle and toward the bearded, cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who holds a cross-staff and blesses his people. An angel holds a canopy over the faithful, while below demons drag sinners away into the fiery pit. The prayer 'save thy people, and bless thine inheritance' shapes the whole drawing.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-27-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-mustair-blessing-children.summary: Christ, seated at the left with a large cross-nimbus, stretches out his hand towards a group of mothers and disciples who bring children to him, set against painted architecture. The scene illustrates Christ's words 'Suffer the little children to come unto me'.
facts: The abbey of Saint John at Müstair, founded c. 780, preserves wall paintings of about 800 arranged in five registers: the life of David at the top, three rows on the youth, ministry and Passion of Christ, and below them scenes of Saint Andrew, joined on the west wall by a Last Judgment.
UNESCO, which inscribed the abbey in 1983, describes them as Switzerland's greatest series of figurative murals, painted around 800.

met:464459.summary: This processional cross of gilded silver over a wooden core shows the crucified Christ in repoussé at its centre, with arms extended along the crossbeam. Rounded terminals at the ends of the arms contain half-length haloed figures, some winged, worked in the same embossed technique, and a knop below fixes the cross to its staff. Carried at the head of processions, it lifted the image of Christ crucified above the gathered faithful.
facts: The Met records an inscription on the obverse giving the name of Jesus Christ.
It was given to the Met in 1917 by J. Pierpont Morgan, and the Met attributes it to 11th-century Spain.
met:464459.notes: Met 17.190.494; 36.2 × 52.7 cm. The terminal figures were not identified by the Met record seen; described cautiously.

walters:71.303.summary: Christ sits within a star-studded mandorla, bearded and frontal, holding a book marked with a cross against his chest, while angels at the upper corners hold the edge of the glory and two small heads appear at its foot. The scheme follows Early Christian book covers of the 6th and 7th centuries. The Walters itself doubts its authenticity, so the plaque may be a later copy of such a model rather than an early medieval work.
facts: The Walters compares the plaque with the Saint-Lupicin Gospel covers in the Bibliothèque nationale and a Saint Paul ivory in the Musée de Cluny, both dated to the 6th–7th century.
The museum notes that the rendering of the eyes, the angels' masked hands, the missing throne and the coarse carving 'cast doubts on the authenticity' of the object, which 'could be a modern copy'.
walters:71.303.notes: Date given by the museum with a question mark ('9th–10th century?'); authenticity questioned by the museum itself. Image viewed on the Walters image server.

Q3877893.summary: In a garden bright with flowers, the risen Christ, carrying a hoe over his shoulder, turns gently from Mary Magdalene as she kneels and reaches toward him. His movement is a kind of dance — he steps away while turning back to her — capturing both the joy of recognition and the call not to cling to him. Painted for a friar's cell, it was meant to lead quiet meditation on the mystery of the Resurrection.
facts: Christ carries a hoe because Mary first mistook him for the gardener.
The small red flowers scattered in the meadow near his feet are sometimes read as echoes of the wounds in his hands and feet.

Fra Angelico and his assistants painted a fresco in each of the friars' cells at San Marco — this one is among the few considered wholly by his own hand — designed as aids to prayer rather than for public display.
